newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Trial of Mujib's killers begins in Bangladesh.
newsitem.headline: Trial of Mujib's killers begins in Bangladesh.

text.p: The trial over the killing of Bangladesh independence leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman opened on Monday, more than 21 years since his death in an army coup and seven months after his daughter became prime minister.

Lawyers said six of the 25 people accused of involvement in the killing of Mujib appeared in court, including three ex-army officers and Zubaida Rashid, wife of retired colonel Abdur Rashid, an alleged mastermind of the revolt.
Abdur Rashid fled Bangladesh after Mujib's daughter, Sheikh Hasina, took over as prime minister last June following an election victory by her father's Awami League party.
No arguments or evidence was presented at Monday's hearing, and the accused will appear in court again on February 22 when a formal hearing over the charges was expected to begin, the lawyers said.
Police have declined to give details of the charges.
Eyewitnesses said the six who appeared in court on Monday were not handcuffed and looked unperturbed, except for Zubaida Rashid.
"Only she was showing some signs of worry," one eyewitness said. "Others looked strong and confident."

In all 32 people, including Mujib, his wife and three sons were killed on August 15, 1975, in the country's first army revolt. Sheikh Hasina and her sister, Sheikh Rehana, survived as they were travelling abroad at the time of the coup.
Police have so far arrested 10 accused, including the three ex-army officers -- Farook Reehman, Shahriar Rashid Khan and Mohammad Khairuzzaman -- and former information minister Taheruddin Thakur.

Six other army officers, suspected masterminds of the coup, were assigned to diplomatic jobs abroad by Mujib's successors -- presidents Khandaker Mushtaque Ahmed and General Ziaur Rahman, husband of former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia.
The six have now absconded. Hasina's government has urged all countries to refuse political asylum or shelter to any of the accused.
Khandaker Mushtaque Ahmed, made president following Mujib's assassination, issued an ordinance protecting the coup leaders from prosecution.
However Bangladesh's parliament in November repealed the ordinance, paving the way for the trial.
